# The cubic PSD objective also has an exact quadrilateral reduction

This is a reduction of an ordinary planar inequality, not its proof.
It retains the six sector areas. In particular it does not assert a Schur
compression of the six-sector matrix into the cubic three-by-three matrix.

## 1. Objective and fixed-sector data

For a convex body with interior source and three balanced spanning normals,
write its positive raw cap areas (q_i), positive coarea section lengths
\(\ell_i\), and total area (k). Set

\[
M=\sum_iq_i/\ell_i,\qquad
f_i=\frac{2\sqrt{kq_i}}{\ell_iM}.
\]

Let (B(f)) have zero diagonal and cyclic off-diagonal entries (f_i/2),
and define (J=\lambda_{\max}(B(f))). The cubic assertion is exactly

\[
J\le1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_i f_i^2+f_1f_2f_3\le4.
\tag{1}
\]

The equivalence, including its positive-boundary cases, is proved in
`candidate d61c49578c90db6d`.

We use the exact fixed-sector feasibility theorem already proved in
`candidate 2e26c63010f03ffc`.
In canonical cyclic coordinates let

\[
R=(A,B,t,a,b,r),\quad
\ell_1=B+b,\quad\ell_2=A+a,\quad\ell_3=t+r.
\]

Fix positive sector areas (W_0,\ldots,W_5), put (c_s=1/(2W_s)), and
use the symmetric six-cycle matrix

\[
L_{ss}=c_{s-1}+c_s-R_s^{-2},\qquad
L_{s,s+1}=c_s-(R_sR_{s+1})^{-1}.
\tag{2}
\]

Actual realization is equivalent to (L\succeq0) and
\(R_sR_{s+1}\le2W_s\). A core edge means equality. The (q_i) and (k)
are fixed linear sums of these areas. Feasible radii form a compact set in
the positive orthant: diagonal inequalities give

\(R_s\ge(c_{s-1}+c_s)^{-1/2}\),

and the core inequalities then bound them above. Hence (J) attains a
maximum at feasible actual data.

## 2. Strict stationary-coordinate gain for the spectral objective

For positive (f), the largest eigenvalue of (B(f)) is simple and has a
positive unit eigenvector (w). Indeed a Rayleigh maximizer can be replaced
by its absolute value; a zero entry propagates along positive edges. Any
other largest-eigenvalue vector must also have one strict sign, since
otherwise taking absolute values strictly improves its Rayleigh quotient.
It cannot be orthogonal to (w), proving simplicity. Thus the largest
eigenvalue is smooth locally, by the simple-root implicit equation.

Keep two inverse chord lengths fixed and vary (x_s=1/\ell_s>0). In the
projective parameter

\[
\tau=\frac{q_sx_s}{q_sx_s+\sum_{j\ne s}q_jx_j},
\]

the selected component of (f) is a positive constant times (\tau),
and the other two are positive constants times (1-\tau). Hence (B(f))
is affine in (\tau). Its largest eigenvalue is convex, as a supremum of
affine Rayleigh quotients.

More strongly, if its first derivative vanishes, **both** sufficiently small
nonzero signs of the parameter change strictly increase (J). Here is a
complete proof. Write (B(\tau+\epsilon)=B_0+\epsilon D). The three edge
derivatives of (D) are nonzero: one is positive and two are negative.
Thus

\[
\det D=\frac{\delta f_1\delta f_2\delta f_3}{4}\ne0.
\]

At stationarity (w^TDw=0), so (z=Dw\ne0) and (z\perp w).
For a fixed sufficiently small (c>0), the Rayleigh quotient of
\(w+\epsilon cz\) at (B_0+\epsilon D\), minus (J(\tau)), has numerator

\[
\epsilon^2\bigl[2c\|z\|^2+
 c^2z^T(B_0-JI)z\bigr]+\epsilon^3c^2z^TDz.
\tag{3}
\]

Choose (c>0) small enough that the bracket is positive. The denominator
is (1+\epsilon^2c^2\|z\|^2>0). Equation (3) is strictly positive for
both sufficiently small signs of (\epsilon\), proving the assertion.

Consequently (J) has exactly the coordinate properties needed below:
one-coordinate projective convexity and strict gain in both directions at
every stationary coordinate. Also it is homogeneous of degree zero in
the chord lengths, so, writing (d_j=\partial J/\partial\ell_j),

\[
\ell_1d_1+\ell_2d_2+\ell_3d_3=0.
\tag{4}
\]

## 3. Applying the fixed-sector extremum mechanism

The geometric matrix perturbations are those fully proved in
`candidate 1a5bfc0fdb9108c3`,
Sections 3–5, 9, and 12. Their objective-dependent inputs are only the
coordinate properties and homogeneity established above. For precision,
the following checks list the entire transfer, including the extra-core
cases.

Increasing a single radius up to its adjacent core bounds increases every
changed entry of (L), retaining its nonpositive off-diagonals. Therefore
PSD persists by the absolute-value quadratic-form comparison. At a maximum,
a chord with (d_j>0) must have a core adjacent to both opposite endpoints.
If all (d_j=0), the strict stationary gain requires every endpoint to touch
a core. Equation (4) therefore implies at least two cores in all cases.

The matrix cannot be positive definite: decreasing any radius then remains
feasible; a negative derivative, or a zero derivative using (3), would
increase the objective. Homogeneity supplies a negative derivative unless
all vanish.

With exactly two cores, select a positive derivative and relabel its chord
as (\ell_1\). The four core patterns and the contradictions that exclude a
PD block are as follows. All exchanges hold the displayed separating core
product fixed, increase entries in the non-PD block, and leave the PD
principal complement positive definite for small changes.

* Cores (0,4): a PD long block has free internal radii (t,a), forcing
  (d_3=d_2=0), contradicting (4). A PD short block allows (A\downarrow,
  B\uparrow\) and (r\downarrow,b\uparrow\), requiring both
  (Ad_2\ge Bd_1>0) and (rd_3\ge bd_1>0), again impossible.
* Cores (1,3): the same argument uses long-block radii (r,A), or the
  short-block exchanges (t\downarrow,B\uparrow\) and
  (a\downarrow,b\uparrow\). The contradictions are identical.
* Cores (0,3): a PD block has free internal radius (t) or (r), forcing
  (d_3=0,d_2<0); its allowed exchange (a\downarrow,b\uparrow\) or
  (A\downarrow,B\uparrow\) then strictly improves the objective.
* Cores (1,4): use the free internal radius (a) or (A), obtaining
  (d_2=0,d_3<0); then exchange (t\downarrow,B\uparrow\) or
  (r\downarrow,b\uparrow\).

Thus both blocks are singular when there are exactly two cores.

Suppose instead there are at least three cores and exactly one singular
connected block. Its size is at most four. The following excludes each
size; PD complements are entire principal submatrices and may contain
additional zero edges.

* A singular singleton at (s): decreasing any of radii (s+2,s+3,s+4)
  does not touch that block and preserves the PD complement. The three
  chord derivatives must therefore all be strictly positive, contradicting
  (4). Zero derivatives are excluded by (3).
* A singular block ({1,2}): decreasing radii 4 and 5 forces
  (d_1,d_3>0), hence (d_2<0). The core-preserving exchange
  (A\downarrow,B\uparrow\) has positive first variation
  (Bd_1-Ad_2).
* A singular block ({0,1,2}): its internal radius (B) can increase,
  forcing (d_1<0). The opposite radius (b) can decrease within the PD
  complement, forcing (d_1>0).
* A singular block ({0,1,2,3}): increasing its internal radii (B,t)
  forces (d_1,d_3<0), hence (d_2>0). Increase (A,a) exponentially and
  decrease (r,b) at the same rate. The separating core products (Ar,ab)
  remain fixed and (br) decreases. The singular block increases entrywise
  and the PD complement stays PD. Its first variation
  ((A+a)d_2-bd_1-rd_3) is positive.

Every case is impossible. Thus at any fixed-sector maximum of (J), the
six-sector matrix has at least two singular connected blocks.

## 4. Exact reconstruction and scope

The sparse-slack reconstruction in
`candidate 9e9a3ee2a80ec95a`
applies independently of the optimized objective. In each PD path block
choose (w=C^{-1}e_j>0), placing positive node slack only at (j); in each
singular block choose its positive null vector. Every positive-excess edge
contributes one inserted polygon vertex and each PD block contributes one
ray vertex. Since there is a core, the graph is a forest and the number of
vertices is exactly (\operatorname{rank}L=6-\#\{\text{singular blocks}\}).
It is therefore at most four here.

The reconstruction preserves every ray endpoint and sector area of the
maximizing data, and hence preserves (J). It is an actual convex body.
This proves:

**Spectral quadrilateral reduction.** Every actual ordinary planar body
with an interior source and balanced three-normal circuit has an actual
triangle or quadrilateral with the same six sector areas and with

\(\lambda_{\max}(B(f))\)

at least as large. In particular, any failure of the cubic PSD inequality
has an actual triangular or quadrilateral witness with the same fixed-line
cap and total areas. Without an incidence hypothesis, both possibilities
remain: the proved triangle cubic theorem concerns distinct-vertex caps,
not arbitrary triangle cuts.

If the original cap fractions satisfy (q_i/k\le128/279), the same holds
after replacement. The proved incidence theorem in
`candidate ca9f00bdb64d6d9e` then makes the
three triangular caps isolate three distinct vertices: its sharp threshold
is (2\sqrt3-3>128/279\). Such a triangle satisfies the cubic inequality
by the audited parameterization (or its weak-incidence closure if needed).
Consequently, under this explicit cap ceiling, a cubic failure has an
actual quadrilateral witness. This conditional conclusion uses no cap
ceiling in the spectral optimization itself.

The optimization may change chord lengths; only the final reconstruction
preserves the maximizing endpoints as well. No neighboring mixed-integer
fiber compatibility is preserved or asserted, and no arbitrary-body cubic
inequality follows without a further quadrilateral proof.
